thread.title_full: Jane Goodall had a message for Floridians: Work together for nature - NewsBreak

author: Max Chesnes
title: Jane Goodall had a message for Floridians: Work together for nature - NewsBreak
text:
By Max Chesnes ,
8 hours ago Jane Goodall in Gombe National Park, Tanzania. Goodall was known for her work with chimpanzees in Gombe, and her observations about chimp behavior have reframed how humans view their place in the natural world. Goodall died Wednesday at 91. [ Courtesy of Shawn Sweeney ] Dr. Jane Goodall, whose groundbreaking chimpanzee observations in Tanzania reshaped how we understand the animal kingdom and our place within it, died Wednesday, according to her global conservation nonprofit. She was 91.
Goodall was not just a force of nature. She was a fearless and unrelenting champion of it. I had the honor of first sitting down in 2023 with Dr. Goodall, a frequent visitor to Florida, ahead of her sold-out lecture for students and educators at the Tampa Theatre.
Our conversation was future-focused and optimistic: We spoke about the countless hours she’d spent among chimpanzees, plans for her upcoming 89th birthday and her tireless work inspiring the next generation of young environmental stewards.
Dr. Jane Goodall speaks to environmental reporter Max Chesnes on Sept. 14, 2024 in St. Petersburg. [ HANNAH FARROW | Times ] But perhaps what stuck with me the most from that initial conversation was her message for Floridians. Our meeting was two years after the peak of a record manatee die-off. Endangered Florida panthers were (and still are) being hit by cars. We, humans, are overpolluting, overbuilding and overconsuming, killing off beloved species along the way. So I asked Goodall:
What’s your message to Floridians about maintaining hope — and fostering change — as we witness the plight of these imperiled species?
This was her full response:
“Without hope, people don’t take action, because what’s the point if it’s not going to work? We do need to know about the doom and gloom, because I think the world is in a horrible mess. But at the same time, I’ve met so many incredible people doing so many wonderful projects — proof that nature is amazingly resilient. If we give her a chance, and maybe a helping hand, places we’ve destroyed can once again become beautiful," she said.
World renowned primatologist, ethologist, and anthropologist Dr. Jane Goodall speaks on stage during a lecture at the Tampa Theatre on March 29, 2023. [ LUIS SANTANA | Times ] Goodall continued: “I think a very important point is: So many animal species on the very brink of extinction have been given another chance because people got together and decided they’re not going to go on our watch. And that can happen here in Florida. If people really care and don’t give up, wonders can be achieved.”
A UN Messenger of Peace, Goodall traveled roughly 300 days a year to speak with the citizens of our one shared Earth — including our government leaders — to inspire hope. Her visits to Tampa Bay drew in thousands of visitors. It is hope, Goodall would say, that will get us through it.
When Goodall returned to the Tampa Bay area last year to speak at Tropicana Field, we reunited for another interview . Amid topics like what drove her to keep traveling at 90, and how she stays connected to nature, I threw in a lighter question based on a comment she made the first time we met.
You told me last time that you like to drink whiskey, I joked. What type of whiskey do you enjoy?
Johnnie Walker black label, Goodall replied with a smile. “My favorite.”
It’s a glass of Johnnie Walker tonight in honor of one of our earth’s biggest advocates. The loss is monumental, but her legacy of hope will endure.
Dr. Jane Goodall speaks to environmental reporter Max Chesnes on Sept. 14, 2024 in St. Petersburg. [ HANNAH FARROW | Hannah Farrow ] Below are select excerpts from the Tampa Bay Times’ recent conversations with Dr. Goodall. The full interview from her 2023 visit can be found here , and the 2024 conversation is here.
As you near your ninth decade on this earth, what motivates you to carry on with your work?
We are, day by day, destroying our environment — upon which we depend. Although some people seem to feel separated from the natural world, we actually aren’t. And because I have grandchildren who could very soon give me great-grandchildren. And because I care passionately about nature and animals. And if we can’t get people inspired to take action, we’re doomed. Literally doomed. We have a window of time, but it’s closing.
Your research with chimpanzees is a gift to this world. You had to break down barriers and face pushback in your early career to accomplish all that you have. What do you say to the next Jane Goodall who may be discouraged by the difficult road that leads to change?
My first pushback came when I was 10 years old. I had read “Tarzan,” and fallen in love with him. (I was really jealous because he married the wrong Jane.) Anyway, that was really what pushed me to make the decision: “I’m going to grow up, go to Africa, live with wild animals and write books about them.” There was no thought of being a scientist because that wasn’t available to girls back then.
But if you really want to do something like this, you’re going to have to work really hard. Take advantage of every opportunity. And then if you don’t give up, hopefully, you find a way. That’s the message I share with young people around the world, particularly in disadvantaged communities.
You spend a lot of time traveling, but are you still able to get away and find time to spend outside?
I get to Tanzania twice a year because my grandchildren are there, for one. And I always get to Gombe . It’s only a few days, but I can get out into the forest. And there I am back in what I consider my natural habitat.
When you speak with these politicians or company leaders, do you feel they’re speaking to you from their heart?
Some are. Others are just greenwashing.
You are a masterful storyteller. How do you use stories as a tool to raise awareness and make change?
Some big, high-up businessman isn’t going to listen to me if I start attacking him. *Laughs* Luckily, stories are just a part of me. It is naturally what I do.
Is there anything that a child or somebody from the younger generations has told you that has really stuck with you?
I got this letter recently, and it was just saying how she wanted to be like me and help animals. And I don’t know why it was so special, but it was. I suddenly realized that she’s in the outskirts of Tampa. (We) tracked down her school and they said, “Oh yes, we know that little girl.”
Well, we’ve managed to get the mother and her child into the lecture tomorrow. Her mother sent us a video of her telling the child and she just she kind of curls up and she starts sobbing. Oh, such an incredible reaction of joy.
Out of pure curiosity: If you had to estimate how many hours in your lifetime you’ve spent with chimpanzees, what would that number be?
I couldn’t begin to count the hours!
How often are you able to reconnect with nature, and are there particular places you like to go where you feel truly connected?
I go back to Tanzania twice a year. It’s not for a great long time, but because I lived there for so long, once I’m back, it all fills up again. But even if I am on tour, and I’m looking out on the road from an airport somewhere, there’s all this cement. And yet little tiny plants will always find a way to start pushing through. It’s truly amazing.
Before we conclude, obviously there’s a lot that you’ve given to this world. What has the world given to you, Dr. Jane Goodall, in return?
It’s given me some wonderful, wonderful times in nature; it’s given me a proper understanding of who animals are, and time to be with them; it’s given me the opportunity to meet some extraordinary people, from all walks of life; it’s given me an opportunity to understand the indomitable spirit that people have; And it’s given me an opportunity to share in the enthusiasm of young people.
